title: De lineis curvis non in eodem plano sitis, quae maximi minimive proprietate sunt praeditae

deep.reconstruction:
Problem III asks for the space curve (x, y(x), z(x)) that makes ∫ X(x) √(dx²+dy²+dz²) stationary, where X is an arbitrary function of x. In modern terms these are geodesics of the conformally flat metric X(x)²(dx²+dy²+dz²), or light rays in a medium whose refractive index depends on one coordinate only.

With p = y', q = z' and s = √(1+p²+q²), the integrand is V = X s.

- Euler's general scheme writes dV = M dx + N dy + N' dz + P dp + P' dq.
- Here N = N' = 0, because y and z do not occur in V.
- P = Xp/s and P' = Xq/s.
- So the two Euler–Lagrange equations for y and z reduce to the first integrals Xp/s = a and Xq/s = b = na.

Dividing the two integrals gives q/p = n, so dz = n dy and z = ny + c. The projection on the yz-plane (BOC) is a straight line, so the whole extremal lies in a plane parallel to the x-axis. This is the cyclic-coordinate, translation-symmetry argument.

Then s = √(1+(1+n²)p²). Solving Xp = a s gives p = a/√(X² − (1+n²)a²). This yields dy = a dx/√(X² − ·a²) and dz = n a dx/√(X² − ·a²).

The next page specialises:
- X = x gives the catenary, i.e. the curve of lowest centre of gravity among isoperimetric curves.
- X = 1/√x gives the brachistochrone.

So the page shows that these classical plane extremals stay plane when the problem is posed in space. It serves the paper's programme of carrying Euler's Methodus inveniendi technique over to curves of double curvature.
errors: Euler sets nn+1 = m, but then writes p = a/√(X² − aamm). From X²p² = a²(1 + (nn+1)p²) the correct result is p = a/√(X² − (nn+1)aa), i.e. X² − m aa, not X² − mm aa. The formulas are consistent if one instead sets nn+1 = mm. The next page (X = 1/√x giving √(1 − mmaax)) uses mm consistently. This is a harmless notational slip in the definition of m, since the constant is arbitrary anyway.

ideas.what: First integrals from the absence of y and z in the integrand: Xp/s = const and Xq/s = const
ideas.modern_name: Conserved momenta for cyclic coordinates (Noether / translation invariance)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Methodus inveniendi, 1744) for the plane case; general formulation by Lagrange and later Noether
ideas.where_published: E65 Methodus inveniendi (plane case); the space-curve extension is in E740 itself

ideas.what: Extremals of ∫X(x)ds in space are planar, lying in a plane parallel to the x-axis
ideas.modern_name: Planarity of rays/geodesics in a stratified (one-dimensional) conformal metric; ray reduction in a layered medium
ideas.usually_credited_to: Folklore of geometric optics (Snell's law in layered media); unsure of a specific attribution
ideas.where_published: Possibly also in Euler's other papers on curves not in one plane (E-numbers near E739/E741); unsure

ideas.what: The catenary and brachistochrone remain the extremals when the problems are posed among space curves
ideas.modern_name: Special cases of the ray equation n(x) sinθ = const

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine application of the Euler–Lagrange equations with cyclic coordinates; the planarity result is elementary and well known. The only notable detail is a minor notational slip (m vs mm).
transcription_corrections: The transcription faithfully reproduces 'nn+1=m' followed by 'aamm' as printed; the misprint or slip is in the original, not the transcription.
In the final displayed formulas the image reads √(X² − mmaa); the transcription is correct.
